title: Energy Conversion and the Conservation of Energy
summary: What energy conversion means, the principle of conservation of energy, and the main forms of energy with their conversions.

p: Energy is part of every physical process: the movement of objects, the working of machines and the functions of living things. One of the most important ideas about energy is that it can change from one form to another. This is called energy conversion. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. An electric iron converts electrical energy into thermal (heat) energy.

sections.h: The principle of conservation of energy
p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system. It can only be changed from one form into another, and the total amount of energy stays the same. So the total energy before a process and the total energy after it are equal, even though the energy may appear in different forms. Machines do not make energy. They only change it.

sections.h: Forms of energy and what they can become
p: Chemical energy: stored in the bonds of chemical substances. It becomes electrical energy in a battery, or thermal and mechanical energy when fuel burns.
Mechanical energy: kinetic energy (energy of motion) and potential energy (energy of position). It becomes electrical energy in a generator and thermal energy through friction.
Electrical energy: energy of moving charges. It becomes mechanical energy in a motor, thermal energy in a heater and light in a bulb.
Thermal energy: energy of the motion of particles. It is made in most conversions, for example by friction, and is often wasted.
Nuclear energy: stored in the nuclei of atoms. In a nuclear reactor it becomes heat and then electrical energy.
Radiant (light) energy: carried by electromagnetic waves. It becomes electrical energy in solar panels and chemical energy in photosynthesis.
Sound energy: energy of vibrating particles, usually made from mechanical energy, for example by a loudspeaker.

title: Examples of Energy Conversion and Energy Transformation Diagrams
summary: Energy conversions in everyday devices and natural processes, drawn as chains of energy transformations.

p: Torchlight: chemical (battery) → electrical → light + heat. Electric fan: electrical → mechanical (rotation). Generator (dynamo): mechanical → electrical. Human body: chemical (food) → mechanical (movement) + thermal (body heat). Hydroelectric dam: potential (water stored high) → kinetic (falling water) → mechanical (turbine) → electrical (generator). Photosynthesis: radiant (sunlight) → chemical (glucose). Car engine: chemical (fuel) → thermal (combustion) → mechanical (movement) → sound + heat (wasted). Microphone: sound → electrical. Loudspeaker: electrical → sound + heat. Electric kettle: electrical → thermal.

title: Efficiency and Energy Loss
summary: Why no machine is 100% efficient, the causes of energy loss, and how to calculate efficiency.

sections.h: Energy is always lost as waste
p: In real systems energy conversion is never 100% efficient. Some energy is always changed into forms we do not want, usually heat. The main causes: friction (mechanical energy turns into heat), resistance in electrical circuits (electrical energy turns into heat), vibration and sound (unwanted noise) and air drag (reduces the efficiency of vehicles and turbines). The wasted energy is not destroyed; it is spread out as heat in the surroundings.

Efficiency shows how much of the input energy becomes useful output energy: Efficiency = (useful energy output ÷ total energy input) × 100%. It can also be written with power: efficiency = (useful power output ÷ power input) × 100%.
An electric filament bulb may change only about 10% of its electrical energy into light. The other 90% is lost as heat. Its efficiency is about 10%.
4 000 J of energy is supplied to a system, and 2 800 J is useful output. Efficiency = (2 800 ÷ 4 000) × 100% = 70%. The wasted energy is 4 000 − 2 800 = 1 200 J.

img.alt: A bar showing 4000 joules of input split into 2800 joules of useful output and 1200 joules wasted, with the efficiency calculation of 70 percent

p: A machine receives 5 000 J and produces 3 500 J of useful work. Efficiency = (3 500 ÷ 5 000) × 100% = 70%.

sections.h: Why a car engine is not 100% efficient
p: Only part of the chemical energy of the fuel becomes the motion of the car. Much is lost as heat through the exhaust and the engine body, as friction between moving parts, as sound and as air drag. A petrol engine is typically about 25 to 30% efficient.

title: Power Transmission: Meaning and Methods
summary: What power transmission is, why it matters, and the mechanical, electrical and hydraulic ways of transmitting energy.

p: Power transmission is the transfer of energy from the place where it is produced (a power station or an engine) to the place where it is used to do work (homes, factories or machines). It makes energy available far from where it is generated.

Its importance: it allows industries, towns and villages to use electricity or mechanical power; energy can be generated in one central plant and used over a wide area; it is cheaper than many small generators, which are costly and hard to maintain; and the networks (grids) join regions and let states or countries share energy.

Energy is passed through physical parts. Belts are flexible loops joining pulleys on different shafts, used in lathes and conveyors. Gears are toothed wheels that interlock and pass motion and force between shafts, used in clocks and engines. Chains and sprockets are used on bicycles and motorcycles.
Advantages: simple and cheap to build. Limitations: parts wear out and the distance is short.

Electrical energy is carried by conductors such as copper or aluminium wires. Overhead cables carry high voltages (for example 132 kV and 330 kV) over long distances. Underground cables are used in towns to avoid ugly wires and hazards.
Advantages: long distances with small loss (especially high-voltage AC), and easy change of voltage with transformers. Limitations: expensive to build; open to weather, vandalism and sabotage.

A pressurised liquid, usually oil, carries the energy. It is used in construction machines, aircraft and presses. Advantages: large forces can be sent through small pipes; control is smooth and exact. Limitations: leaks can be dangerous; it works over short distances and moderate speeds.

p: Alternating current (AC) changes direction periodically. Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only. Power stations in Nigeria and homes use AC.

p: Transformers work only with alternating current. The voltage can be stepped up for economical transmission and stepped down for safe use. DC from batteries or solar panels cannot be changed by a transformer because the current in the coil is steady and does not produce a changing magnetic field.

title: Transformers
summary: How a transformer works, the difference between step-up and step-down transformers, the transformer equations and worked examples.

p: A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current by electromagnetic induction. It has two coils of wire, the primary and the secondary, wound on a soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the core. This field induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil.

img.alt: A transformer with a primary coil of 400 turns, a secondary coil of 40 turns on an iron core, and the equation Vp over Vs equals Np over Ns equals Is over Ip
img.cap: A step-down transformer: 150 V in, 15 V out.

p: A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary than in the primary (Ns > Np). It raises the voltage and lowers the current. It is used at power stations to prepare electricity for long-distance transmission. A step-down transformer has fewer turns in the secondary (Ns < Np). It lowers the voltage and raises the current. It is used near homes and factories.
In an ideal transformer, power in = power out, because energy is conserved: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. So if the voltage is stepped down, the current is stepped up in the same ratio.
Vp / Vs = Np / Ns = Is / Ip (ideal transformer, 100% efficient), where Vp and Vs are the primary and secondary voltages, Np and Ns the numbers of turns, and Ip and Is the currents.
Primary 400 turns, secondary 40 turns, input 150 V. Vp / Vs = Np / Ns: 150 / Vs = 400 / 40 = 10, so Vs = 15 V.
Primary 100 turns, secondary 200 turns, primary voltage 100 V. Np < Ns, so it is a step-up transformer. Vs = 100 × 200 / 100 = 200 V.

The 150 V to 15 V transformer in Example 1 takes 0.5 A from the supply. Power in = 150 × 0.5 = 75 W. In an ideal transformer the output current is Is = 75 / 15 = 5 A. The current is stepped up 10 times as the voltage is stepped down 10 times.
A transformer has 400 turns in the primary and 100 in the secondary and a primary voltage of 240 V. Vs = 240 × 100 / 400 = 60 V (step-down).

title: Why Power Is Transmitted at High Voltage
summary: Power loss in cables (P = I²R), why high voltage reduces loss, a worked example and problems of power transmission in Nigeria.

p: A cable has resistance R. When a current I flows, the power lost as heat is P(loss) = I²R. Because the loss depends on the square of the current, a small reduction in current gives a big reduction in loss.

Power sent = voltage × current (P = IV). For the same power, a higher voltage means a smaller current. So transmitting at high voltage reduces the loss. That is why step-up transformers are used at power stations.
A generator rated 12 kW, 2 kV sends power through a cable of resistance 20 Ω. Find the power loss. I = P / V = 12 000 / 2 000 = 6 A. Power loss = I²R = 6² × 20 = 36 × 20 = 720 W.

Now step the voltage up to 20 kV. I = 12 000 / 20 000 = 0.6 A. Power loss = 0.6² × 20 = 0.36 × 20 = 7.2 W. Raising the voltage 10 times made the current 10 times smaller and the loss 100 times smaller.
Transformers keep the voltage steady at different points in the grid: stepped up for the long-distance lines and stepped down at substations for homes and factories.

sections.h: Problems of power transmission in Nigeria
p: Vandalism of cables and towers, theft of conductors, bush fires and weather damage; long lines that pass through remote areas and give losses; poor maintenance and old equipment; and the high cost of building and protecting lines. These cause blackouts and reduce industrial output. Environmental problems include clearing forests for line routes and the danger of fallen lines and electrocution in rural villages.

title: Machines: Meaning, Functions and Classes
summary: What a machine is, what machines do, and the simple machines (lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle) and compound machines.

p: A machine is a device that makes work easier. It can multiply force, change the direction of a force, or increase speed or distance. A machine does not create energy; it only helps us use available energy more conveniently.

Simple machines are basic mechanical devices. The lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fulcrum. There are three classes: first class (fulcrum between load and effort: seesaw, crowbar), second class (load between fulcrum and effort: wheelbarrow, nutcracker) and third class (effort between fulcrum and load: forearm, fishing rod).

img.alt: Diagrams of the three classes of lever with the load, effort and fulcrum marked

p: A pulley is a grooved wheel with a rope. A fixed pulley changes the direction of the force. A movable pulley multiplies the force. A block and tackle is a combination of pulleys. An inclined plane (ramp) is a sloping surface used to raise heavy objects. A wedge tapers to a thin edge and is used for splitting (an axe). A screw is an inclined plane wound round a cylinder. A wheel and axle is a large wheel fixed to a small axle (a door handle, a car steering wheel).

A compound machine has two or more simple machines working together: a wheelbarrow (lever + wheel and axle), a crane (pulley + lever), scissors (two levers + a wedge) and a bicycle (wheel and axle + levers + gears). In real machines, efficiency is always less than 100% because of friction, heat and deformation.

title: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency of Machines
summary: The formulas for mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency of a machine, with corrected worked examples.

p: Mechanical advantage (MA) = load ÷ effort. It tells how many times the machine multiplies the force.

Velocity ratio (VR) = distance moved by the effort ÷ distance moved by the load. For a block and tackle, VR equals the number of rope sections supporting the load. For an inclined plane, VR = length of slope ÷ vertical height. For a wheel and axle, VR = radius of the wheel ÷ radius of the axle.
Efficiency = (MA ÷ VR) × 100%. It is also (work output ÷ work input) × 100%. MA is never greater than VR.
A load of 100 N is lifted by an effort of 20 N. MA = 100 / 20 = 5.
A machine has VR = 4 and MA = 3. Efficiency = (3 / 4) × 100% = 75%.

sections.h: Example 3: a machine with the numbers corrected
p: A machine lifts a 500 N load through 2 m when the effort moves 6 m. VR = 6 / 2 = 3. (A printed exercise says the effort is 125 N, but then MA = 500 / 125 = 4, which is more than VR. This is impossible because it would give an efficiency of 133%.) With an effort of 200 N, MA = 500 / 200 = 2.5 and efficiency = (2.5 / 3) × 100% = 83.3%.
Check with work: work output = 500 × 2 = 1 000 J. Work input = 200 × 6 = 1 200 J. Efficiency = 1 000 / 1 200 = 83.3%.
A system of pulleys has 4 rope sections supporting the load, so VR = 4. An effort of 125 N lifts a load of 400 N. MA = 400 / 125 = 3.2. Efficiency = 3.2 / 4 × 100% = 80%.
A 5 m long ramp rises 1 m. VR = 5. A load of 500 N is pushed up with an effort of 125 N. MA = 4. Efficiency = 4 / 5 × 100% = 80%.
